results.title: Elements with the same powered congruence differ by inertia

results.title: Powers of a Frobenius map satisfy the powered congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Powers of an arithmetic Frobenius map satisfy the powered congruence: if `φ x - x ^ q ∈ Q` for all `x`, then `(φ ^ f) x - x ^ q ^ f ∈ Q`.

results.title: Powers of a Frobenius element satisfy the powered congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Powers of an arithmetic Frobenius element satisfy the powered congruence: if `σ • x - x ^ q ∈ Q` for all `x`, with `q = Nat.card (R ⧸ Q.under R)`, then `(σ ^ f) • x - x ^ q ^ f ∈ Q`.

results.title: Restriction of a Frobenius element along a compatible pair
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A Frobenius congruence restricts along a compatible pair: if `ι : C →ₐ[R] B` and `ρ : G →* H` satisfy `ι (ρ g • c) = g • ι c`, and `σ` is a Frobenius at `Q`, then `ρ σ` is a Frobenius at `Q.comap ι`.

results.title: Uniqueness of Frobenius powers with trivial inertia
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `σ` is a Frobenius at `Q` and `τ` satisfies the powered congruence with exponent `q ^ f`, then `σ ^ f = τ` when the inertia subgroup of `Q` is trivial. This is a uniqueness helper for an already supplied powered congruence. The actual tower theorem below derives that congruence from the Frobenius premise over the intermediate ring and its residue cardinality.

results.title: Restriction of Frobenius equals Frobenius with trivial inertia
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `σ` is a Frobenius at `Q` and `τ` satisfies the Frobenius congruence at `Q.comap ι`, then `ρ σ = τ` when the inertia subgroup of `Q.comap ι` is trivial. This is the equality form of the restriction statement of Proposition 7.22 under its unramified hypothesis.

results.title: Intermediate residue cardinality as a power of the base residue cardinality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a finite ring tower `R → T → B`, the intermediate prime residue quotient has cardinality equal to the base residue cardinality raised to its canonical inertia degree. The cardinality theorem is Mathlib's `cardQuot_pow_inertiaDeg`.

results.title: Frobenius in a tower is a power of the base Frobenius
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a finite ring tower `R → T → B`, the Frobenius over `T`, embedded into an action over `R`, equals the Frobenius over `R` raised to the intermediate residue degree when the inertia subgroup is trivial. Only `H` must fix `T`.

results.title: Frobenius tower equality for algebra automorphisms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For algebra automorphisms in a finite ring tower, the inclusion of the intermediate Frobenius is the canonical `AlgEquiv.restrictScalars`.

results.title: Frobenius tower equality for an intermediate field
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The tower equality for the source's intermediate field `E ⊂ L`. Here `K` is the fraction field of the base ring `R`, `T` is the integral closure of `R` in `E`, and `B` is its integral closure in `L`. In the number-field application these are the three rings of integers. The intermediate action is `E.fixingSubgroup`; the whole `Gal(L/K)` need not fix `T`.

results.caption: Definition

results.title: First coordinate of the fundamental negative Pell solution
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, let $Y$ be the least positive integer $y$ such that $x^2 - d y^2 = -1$ for some integer $x$, or $0$ if there is no such $y$. Then $X = \lfloor \sqrt{d Y^2 - 1} \rfloor$, where $d Y^2 - 1$ is read as $0$ when $d Y^2 = 0$. So $X$ is the nonnegative integer with $X^2 - d Y^2 = -1$ when a solution exists, and $X = 0$ otherwise.

results.title: Comparison of the negative Pell sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d > 1$ be a natural number such that $x^2 - d y^2 = -1$ has an integer solution, let $(X, Y)$ be its fundamental solution (the one with $X, Y > 0$ and $Y$ least), and write $(X + Y \sqrt{d})^n = f_n + g_n \sqrt{d}$. results.title: Primes with strictly primitive representations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an integer $d$, $S(d)$ is the set of primes $p$ for which there is an integer $l > 0$ such that $|x^2 - d y^2| = p^l$ has a strictly primitive integral solution, that is, integers $x, y$ with $x$ and $d y$ coprime.

results.title: Strictly primitive exponent
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $d$ be an integer and $p$ a natural number, and let $S(d)$ be the set of primes $q$ for which $|x^2 - d y^2| = q^l$ has a strictly primitive integral solution (integers $x, y$ with $x$ and $d y$ coprime) for some integer $l > 0$. If $p \in S(d)$, then $l_p$ is the least integer $l > 0$ such that $|x^2 - d y^2| = p^l$ has a strictly primitive integral solution; if $p \notin S(d)$, then $l_p = 0$.

results.title: Vanishing of the strictly primitive exponent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ be an integer and let $S(d)$ be the set of primes $p$ for which $|x^2 - d y^2| = p^l$ has a strictly primitive integral solution ($x$ and $d y$ coprime) for some integer $l > 0$. Let $l_p$ be the least such $l$ when $p \in S(d)$, and $l_p = 0$ otherwise. Then $l_p = 0$ for every natural number $p \notin S(d)$, in particular for every $p$ that is not prime.

results.title: The strictly primitive exponent is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ be an integer and let $S(d)$ be the set of primes $p$ for which $|x^2 - d y^2| = p^l$ has a strictly primitive integral solution ($x$ and $d y$ coprime) for some integer $l > 0$; for $p \in S(d)$ let $l_p$ be the least such $l$. Then for every $p \in S(d)$, $l_p > 0$ and $|x^2 - d y^2| = p^{l_p}$ has a strictly primitive integral solution.

results.title: Minimality of the strictly primitive exponent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ be an integer and let $S(d)$ be the set of primes $p$ for which $|x^2 - d y^2| = p^l$ has a strictly primitive integral solution ($x$ and $d y$ coprime) for some integer $l > 0$; for $p \in S(d)$ let $l_p$ be the least such $l$. If $p \in S(d)$ and $l > 0$ is an integer for which $|x^2 - d y^2| = p^l$ has a strictly primitive integral solution, then $l_p \le l$.

results.title: Parameter interval of unit arcs
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Planar arcs are parametrized by the closed unit interval $[0, 1]$ of real numbers.

results.title: Unit arc
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A unit arc is a continuous map $\gamma$ from the closed interval $[0, 1]$ to the complex plane whose length, the total variation of $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$, equals $1$.

results.title: Direct rigid motion of the plane
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real angle $\theta$ and a complex number $\tau$, the motion with angle $\theta$ and translation $\tau$ sends $z \in \mathbb{C}$ to $e^{i\theta} z + \tau$: a rotation about the origin by $\theta$ followed by translation by $\tau$, with neither reflection nor rescaling.

results.title: Direct rigid motions of the plane are isometries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real angle $\theta$ and every complex number $\tau$, the map $z \mapsto e^{i\theta} z + \tau$ of the complex plane is an isometry: it preserves the distance $|z - w|$ between any two points $z, w \in \mathbb{C}$.

results.title: Straight path
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The straight path is the continuous map from the interval $[0, 1]$ to the complex plane that sends each $t \in [0, 1]$ to $t$ viewed as a complex number; it traces the segment from $0$ to $1$.

results.title: The identity on the unit interval has total variation one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The total variation of the inclusion $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$, $t \mapsto t$, over the whole interval $[0, 1]$ equals $1$.

results.title: The straight segment has length one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The path $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$, $t \mapsto t$, which traces the segment from $0$ to $1$ on the real axis, has total variation (length) exactly $1$ over $[0, 1]$.

results.title: Straight unit arc
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The straight unit arc is the unit arc whose curve is the straight path $t \mapsto t$ from $[0, 1]$ to the complex plane, which traces the segment from $0$ to $1$ and has length $1$.

results.title: Sets that cover every unit arc
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ covers every unit arc when for every unit arc $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$, that is, every continuous map whose total variation (length) is exactly $1$, there are an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a translation $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $e^{i\theta} \gamma(t) + \tau \in \Omega$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$.

results.title: Sets covering every unit arc are nonempty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ covers every unit arc, that is, contains a rotated and translated copy of every continuous curve $[0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly one, then $\Omega$ is nonempty.

results.title: The empty set does not cover every unit arc
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The empty set $\emptyset \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ does not cover every unit arc: not every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ can be mapped into $\emptyset$ by a rotation followed by a translation.

results.title: Convex universal covers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a convex universal cover when it is nonempty, convex (as a subset of the real plane $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$), and covers every unit arc: for every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ there are $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$ with $e^{i\theta} \gamma(t) + \tau \in \Omega$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$.

results.title: Universal covers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a universal cover when it is nonempty and covers every unit arc: for every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ there are $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\tau \in \mathbb{C}$ with $e^{i\theta} \gamma(t) + \tau \in \Omega$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$. Neither convexity nor measurability of $\Omega$ is required.

results.title: Convex universal covers are null-measurable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a convex universal cover of unit arcs, then $\Omega$ is a null-measurable set for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C}$.

results.title: Convex universal covers are universal covers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every convex universal cover $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a universal cover.

results.title: Areas of convex universal covers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set of convex cover areas is the set of all values $\operatorname{vol}(\Omega) \in [0, \infty]$, where $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ ranges over the convex universal covers and $\operatorname{vol}$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$.

results.title: Areas of universal covers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set of values $\lambda(\Omega) \in [0, \infty]$, where $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ ranges over the universal covers and $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$, applied as an outer measure since $\Omega$ need not be measurable.

results.title: Infimal area of convex universal covers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The convex cover area infimum is the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the set of convex cover areas, that is, the infimum of the Lebesgue areas of all convex universal covers $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$.

results.title: Infimal area of a universal cover
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the areas $\lambda(\Omega)$ of the universal covers $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$, applied as an outer measure since $\Omega$ need not be measurable.

results.title: The closed unit disk covers every unit arc
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every continuous curve $\gamma : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{C}$ of length exactly $1$ there are an angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a translation $c \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $|e^{i\theta}\gamma(t) + c| \le 1$ for every $t \in [0, 1]$; that is, the closed disk of radius $1$ centred at $0$ covers every unit arc.

results.title: The closed unit disk is a convex universal cover
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The closed disk $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| \le 1\}$ is a convex universal cover: it is nonempty, convex, and covers every unit arc.

results.title: The set of convex cover areas is nonempty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of convex cover areas, the Lebesgue areas of all convex universal covers in $\mathbb{C}$, is nonempty; that is, some convex universal cover exists.

results.title: The set of universal cover areas is nonempty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of values $\lambda(\Omega) \in [0, \infty]$, where $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ ranges over the universal covers and $\lambda$ is Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$, is nonempty.

results.title: The infimal area of convex universal covers is finite
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The convex cover area infimum, the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the Lebesgue areas of all convex universal covers in $\mathbb{C}$, is not $\infty$.

results.title: The infimal area of universal covers is finite
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The cover area infimum, the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the Lebesgue areas of all universal covers in $\mathbb{C}$ (nonempty sets that cover every unit arc, not necessarily convex), is not $\infty$.

results.title: Moser's convex worm cover constant
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The convex worm cover constant is the real number obtained from the convex cover area infimum, the infimum in $[0, \infty]$ of the Lebesgue areas of all convex universal covers in $\mathbb{C}$, by the conversion $[0, \infty] \to \mathbb{R}$ that is the identity on finite values and sends $\infty$ to $0$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The convex worm cover constant is at least $0$.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the nonconvex worm cover constant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The nonconvex worm cover constant is greater than or equal to $0$.

results.title: The nonconvex worm cover constant is at most the convex one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The nonconvex worm cover constant (the infimal area of universal covers of unit arcs) is less than or equal to the convex worm cover constant (the infimal area of convex universal covers of unit arcs).

results.title: Disk of radius one half
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The closed disk $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| \le 1/2\}$ of radius $1/2$ centred at $0$.

results.title: Semidisk of radius one half
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The closed upper half-disk $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| \le 1/2,\ \operatorname{Im} z \ge 0\}$ of radius $1/2$ centred at $0$.

results.title: Wetzel's sector
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the closed circular sector of radius $1$ and opening angle $30^\circ$ with apex at the origin, placed symmetrically about the positive real axis: the set of complex numbers $z$ with $|z| \le 1$, $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$ and $|\operatorname{Im} z| \le \tan(\pi/12) \operatorname{Re} z$.

results.title: Centered unit segment
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Hanner cube
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cube $C_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is defined by recursion on $n$: $C_0$ is the centered unit segment $[-1, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^1$, and $C_{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is the $\ell_\infty$ sum of $C_n$ and the centered unit segment.

results.title: Hanner cross-polytope
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cross-polytope $P_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is defined by recursion on $n$: $P_0$ is the centered unit segment $[-1, 1] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^1$, and $P_{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is the $\ell_1$ sum of $P_n$ and the centered unit segment.

results.title: The Hanner cubes are Hanner polytopes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Hanner cube $C_n \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a Hanner polytope.

results.title: The Hanner cross-polytopes are Hanner polytopes

results.title: Membership in the Hanner unit segment
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Membership in the $\ell_\infty$ Hanner sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ and $L \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. A point $x \in \mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ lies in the $\ell_\infty$ Hanner sum of $K$ and $L$ if and only if $(x_1, \dots, x_m) \in K$ and $(x_{m+1}, \dots, x_{m+n}) \in L$.

results.title: Hanner polytopes are convex

results.summary: Let $p, q$ be points of a pseudometric space $E$ with distance $d$. We say that $c$ is the metric center of $(p, q)$ when $c \in R_n$ for every $n$, and every point $y \in E$ with $y \in R_n$ for every $n$ equals $c$.

results.title: Euclidean distance set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the distance set of $E$ is $\Delta(E) = \{\lvert x - y \rvert : x, y \in E\}$, the set of Euclidean distances between pairs of points of $E$.

results.title: Planar Falconer threshold property
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An element $s \in [0, \infty]$ has the planar threshold property when every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s$ has a distance set $\{|x - y| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

results.title: Admissible planar threshold
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An extended nonnegative real $s$ is an admissible planar threshold when $0 \le s \le 2$ and $s$ has the planar threshold property: every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s$ has a distance set of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

results.title: Planar distance threshold
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The planar distance threshold is the infimum, taken in $[0, \infty]$, of the admissible planar thresholds, that is, of all $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact subset $E$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than $s$ has a distance set of positive Lebesgue measure.

results.title: Distances are nonnegative
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, the distance set of $E$ is contained in $[0, \infty)$.

results.title: Distance set of the empty set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $d$, the distance set of the empty subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$ is empty.

results.title: Distance set of a singleton
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every point $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the distance set of $\{x\}$ is $\{0\}$.

results.title: Distance sets of compact sets are compact
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is compact, then the distance set of $E$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

results.title: Distance sets of compact sets are Borel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is compact, then the distance set of $E$ is a Borel measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

results.title: The planar threshold property is upward closed
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s \le t$ be elements of $[0, \infty]$. If $s$ has the planar threshold property, that is, every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s$ has a distance set of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, then $t$ has the planar threshold property.

results.title: Subsets of the plane have Hausdorff dimension at most two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every subset $E$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $\dim_H E \le 2$.

results.title: Two is an admissible planar threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The number $2$ is an admissible planar threshold: $2 \in [0, 2]$, and every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > 2$ has a distance set of positive Lebesgue measure. This holds vacuously, since no subset of the plane has Hausdorff dimension greater than $2$.

results.title: Admissible planar thresholds exist
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an admissible planar threshold, that is, the set of admissible planar thresholds is nonempty.

results.title: Admissible thresholds bound the planar distance threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $s \in [0, \infty]$ that is an admissible planar threshold, the planar distance threshold is at most $s$.

results.title: The planar distance threshold is at most two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The planar distance threshold is at most $2$.

results.title: The planar distance threshold is finite
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The planar distance threshold, an element of $[0, \infty]$, is not $\infty$.

results.title: Real round trip of the planar distance threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\tau \in [0, \infty]$ be the planar distance threshold and let $\tau_{\mathbb{R}}$ be its value as a real number (with the convention that $\infty$ goes to $0$). Viewing $\tau_{\mathbb{R}}$ again as an element of $[0, \infty]$ gives back $\tau$.

results.title: Trivial lower bound for the planar distance threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The planar distance threshold is at least $0$.

results.title: Thresholds up to two with the planar threshold property bound the planar distance threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Thresholds up to two with the planar threshold property bound the planar distance threshold. For every $s \in [0, \infty]$ with $s \le 2$ that has the planar threshold property, the planar distance threshold is at most $s$.

results.title: Zero-measure distance sets give lower bounds for the planar distance threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \in [0, \infty]$. If $E$ is a compact subset of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E$ satisfies $t \le \dim_H E$ and whose distance set has Lebesgue measure zero, then $t$ is at most the planar distance threshold.

results.title: Real form of admissible planar thresholds
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real number $s \ge 0$, $s$ is an admissible planar threshold (as an element of $[0, \infty]$) if and only if $s \in [0, 2]$ and $s$ has the planar threshold property.

results.title: The planar distance threshold is itself a threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s_0 \in [0, \infty]$ be the planar distance threshold, the infimum of the admissible planar thresholds. Every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension $\dim_H E > s_0$ has a distance set of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

results.title: The planar distance threshold is admissible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The planar distance threshold is an admissible planar threshold: it lies in $[0, 2]$ and has the planar threshold property.

results.title: The planar distance threshold is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The planar distance threshold is the least admissible planar threshold: it is itself an admissible planar threshold, and it is at most every admissible planar threshold.

results.title: Real form of the admissible threshold family
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The set of real numbers $r \in [0, 2]$ such that $r$, viewed as an element of $[0, \infty]$, has the planar threshold property equals the image of the set of admissible planar thresholds under the map $[0, \infty] \to \mathbb{R}$ that is the identity on finite values and sends $\infty$ to $0$.

results.title: The planar distance threshold as a real infimum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The value of the planar distance threshold as a real number (with the convention that $\infty$ goes to $0$) equals the infimum in $\mathbb{R}$ of the set of real numbers $r \in [0, 2]$ that, as elements of $[0, \infty]$, have the planar threshold property.

results.title: Statement of Falconer's distance set theorem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the proposition that for every integer $d \ge 2$ and every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ whose Hausdorff dimension is strictly greater than $(d+1)/2$, the distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ has positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

results.title: Wolff's planar distance set condition, as a proposition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with Hausdorff dimension greater than $4/3$ has a distance set $\{|x - y| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive Lebesgue measure.

results.title: Statement of the Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang planar distance set theorem

results.summary: This is the proposition that $5/4$ has the planar threshold property: every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ whose Hausdorff dimension is strictly greater than $5/4$ has a distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

results.title: Statement of Falconer's measure-zero distance set examples
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the proposition that for every integer $d \ge 2$ and every $s$ with $0 \le s \le d/2$, there is a compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of Hausdorff dimension exactly $s$ whose distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

results.title: Statement of the upper bound $3/2$ for the planar distance threshold
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the proposition that the planar distance threshold, the infimum of all $s \in [0, 2]$ such that every compact set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of Hausdorff dimension strictly greater than $s$ has a distance set $\{\|x - y\| : x, y \in E\}$ of positive one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, is at most $3/2$.

results.title: Parking function
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Lower-tail characterization of parking functions

results.title: Number of partial parking functions

A partial parking function with $s$ cars and $t$ spots is a map $f : \{0, \dots, s - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, t - 1\}$ such that for every spot $k \in \{0, \dots, t - 1\}$ at most $t - k$ cars $i$ have $f(i) \ge k$. The number of partial parking functions with $s$ cars and $t$ spots is $(t + 1 - s)(t + 1)^{s - 1}$.
